whyThisMatters: A lot of what feels true about invoices, wires, and vendor payments is only partly right — and Accounts is targeted precisely because so many checks get skipped when a request already looks routine. A few minutes here will clear up what really matters when an invoice, a refund ask, or a payment request already looks normal.
rememberThis: This month's reminder: familiar packaging is not proof. A matching invoice format, a senior name, or an urgent deadline can all be faked — check the sender's exact domain and verify any bank-detail change on a number you already have, every time.

discussionPrompts: Ask if anyone has ever paid an invoice faster because the format and logo looked exactly right — what would make them check the bank details separately next time?
For the overpayment myth, ask how long it would actually take to check the claim against your own ledger versus just refunding it.
Ask the group to name their own trusted way to verify a bank-detail change — is it written down anywhere, or does everyone do it differently?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often get the overpayment myth wrong. Refunding quickly feels helpful and low-risk, so many people say it's fine to just send the difference back. But checking your own ledger first takes minutes, and skipping that check is exactly how the scam works.

items.myth: If an invoice looks correctly formatted and matches the usual layout, it's safe to pay as instructed.
items.fact: A correctly-formatted invoice with changed bank details is the single most common invoice-fraud pattern — the layout being right proves nothing about who is really asking for payment.
items.detail: Always verify a bank-detail change on a number you already have for that vendor, never a number or reply address the invoice itself supplies, no matter how routine the invoice looks.

items.myth: Fraudulent wire-transfer requests always come from obviously fake, poorly-written emails.
items.fact: The most convincing requests come from domains that are nearly identical to the real one, written in polished, professional language — a senior name and a confident tone are what make them work, not sloppy writing.
items.detail: A request that asks you to stay quiet or skip the normal approval process is the real warning sign — not typos, and not the amount involved.

items.myth: If a vendor says you overpaid them, the fastest and safest thing to do is refund the difference right away.
items.fact: A claimed overpayment should always be checked against your own ledger first — attackers invent overpayments specifically to get you to send money to a "corrected" account you don't recognise.
items.detail: Reversing a payment after the fact is far harder than pausing before you send one, so the few minutes it takes to check your own records is always worth it.

items.myth: A tight deadline on a payment or bank-detail change request is just normal business pressure.
items.fact: An artificial deadline is one of the most reliable signs of payment fraud — a genuine vendor or colleague rarely needs a same-day bank-detail change badly enough to skip your normal process.
items.detail: Treat any request that pairs urgency with a bank-detail change or an unusual payment as the pattern to check first, before you act on the deadline.

items.myth: A financial statement attachment is safe to open as long as it's from a vendor you already recognise.
items.fact: An attachment needing "Enable Content" to open, or with a double file ending like .pdf.exe, should never be opened — regardless of how familiar the sender's name looks.
items.detail: Check the sender's exact domain letter by letter before opening anything financial, since a familiar vendor name is easy to spoof alongside a malicious attachment.

items.myth: Replying to the same email to confirm a bank-detail change is a reasonable way to double-check it.
items.fact: Replying to the same email only confirms the address is active — it never verifies who is actually behind it, since an attacker controlling that inbox will simply reply back to confirm.
items.detail: The only real check is a callback on a number you already had for that vendor or colleague before this request, never a contact detail the request itself supplies.
